lesson.title: Git objects commits branches and remotes
lesson.why: Git commands are easier to reason about when commits are immutable snapshots and branches are movable names. This model explains why fetching does not automatically replace your files and why an uncommitted edit is not safely stored in history.
lesson.what: Git stores content-addressed objects and references. The working tree holds editable files, the index prepares the next snapshot and commits connect snapshots into a parent graph. Remotes identify other repositories, not a magical central copy.

concepts.name: Object types
concepts.body: Blobs store file content, trees connect names to blobs and subtrees, and commits reference a tree plus parents and metadata. Content-addressing detects object changes. A commit identifier names the recorded object, not a continuously updating version of a file.

concepts.name: Index and working tree
concepts.body: Staging copies selected content into the index. Editing a file after staging does not automatically update that staged copy. Compare unstaged and staged differences separately so the next commit contains the intended snapshot rather than whatever currently appears in the editor.

concepts.name: Branches and HEAD
concepts.body: A branch is a reference to a commit. HEAD normally names the checked-out branch, which moves when committing. Detached HEAD names a commit directly; new commits can still be created, but should receive a branch name before switching away.

concepts.name: Remote-tracking references
concepts.body: Fetch downloads objects and updates configured remote-tracking references without merging them into the current branch. Origin is a conventional remote name, not a special server. Push requests reference updates elsewhere and can be rejected by permissions or history constraints.

e2e: Edit a working-tree file and inspect its unstaged difference.
Stage the intended content and review the index snapshot.
Create a commit whose parent connects it to existing history.
Fetch or push through configured remotes while explicitly choosing how histories should integrate.

tasks.name: Create an isolated repository
steps: In Bash, choose a fresh disposable parent and run `git init git-object-demo; cd git-object-demo; printf 'one\n' > note.txt; git add note.txt; git -c user.name=Demo -c user.email=demo@example.invalid commit -m first`. Expect one root commit; no remote is configured.

tasks.name: Compare staged content
steps: Inside that demo run `printf 'two\n' > note.txt; git add note.txt; printf 'three\n' > note.txt`. Run `git diff --cached` and `git diff`. Expect staged one-to-two and unstaged two-to-three changes, demonstrating two distinct snapshots.

tasks.name: Inspect object relationships
steps: Run `git cat-file -p HEAD` and `git ls-tree HEAD` in the demo. Identify the commit's tree and note.txt's blob reference. Hash values vary; explain why the commit still represents one even though the working file now contains three.

tasks.name: Reason about a fetch
steps: Offline, draw local main at A and a remote-tracking main moving from A to B after fetch. Local main stays at A until a separate integration step. Explain why this lets you inspect incoming changes before modifying your checked-out history.

key_terms: Blob: stored file content.
Tree: named snapshot entries.
Index: proposed next commit snapshot.
Reference: name pointing to a Git object.
lesson.safety: Run mutations only inside the newly created demo repository. Do not configure a remote or change global Git identity.
cleanup: Inspect the demo path and remove only git-object-demo when finished; no push or external repository change is required.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical developer stages a file, edits it again and commits. Which version is recorded, and how can they check?
interview_points: The index supplies the committed snapshot.
Unstaged edits remain outside that commit.
Compare git diff and git diff --cached.
Understand branches as names pointing to immutable commits.

git/git-objects-commits-branches-and-rem.core: Working tree, index and commit are distinct snapshots. Commits reference trees and parents; branches are movable names. Fetch updates remote-tracking information without automatically integrating it into your current branch.
objectives: Predict staged versus unstaged commit content.
prerequisites: Have Git and a disposable working directory; Bash for the optional commands.

storyboard.title: The staged file differs from the working file
storyboard.objective: Trace the snapshot that a commit actually records.

scenes.title: Stage version two
scenes.caption: The index receives the selected file contents.
scenes.narration: Git add copies version two into the index, which becomes the proposed snapshot for the next commit.

scenes.title: Edit version three
scenes.caption: Later edits do not automatically replace staged contents.
scenes.narration: The developer changes the working file again. The index still contains version two while the editor displays version three.

scenes.title: Review and commit
scenes.caption: Compare staged and unstaged differences deliberately.
scenes.narration: The developer reviews both differences and commits the index, preserving version two unless the newer edit is staged first.

lesson.title: Git merge rebase and conflict resolution
lesson.why: Combining histories is not just making conflict markers disappear. The final code must preserve both branches' intent, and the chosen integration method must respect whether other people already depend on existing commit identities.
lesson.what: Merge connects histories, usually retaining their existing commits. Rebase replays selected changes onto a new base and creates new commit identities. Both can stop for conflicts where Git cannot safely combine changes automatically.

concepts.name: Merge topology
concepts.body: A divergent merge can create a commit with two parents. A fast-forward simply advances a reference when no divergence exists. Keeping history topology can explain parallel development, but successful textual merging does not prove semantic compatibility between the changes.

concepts.name: Rebase identities
concepts.body: Rebase applies changes as new commits on another base. Parent or metadata differences change commit identities even when a patch looks identical. Rewriting a shared branch forces collaborators to reconcile old and new histories, so follow the team's published-history policy.

concepts.name: Conflict meaning
concepts.body: Conflict markers show alternative text, not a ranking of correctness. Understand both intended behaviors and surrounding interfaces before editing. During rebase, labels such as ours and theirs can be counterintuitive because the operation is replaying commits onto a different base.

concepts.name: Recovery and verification
concepts.body: Inspect status to identify the active operation. After resolving, stage intended files and continue that operation. Merge and rebase provide abort paths; use them when uncertain rather than guessing. Run behavior-focused tests because conflict-free code can still be wrong.

e2e: Start with a clean or deliberately saved working tree and inspect both histories.
Choose merge or rebase according to collaboration policy and desired history.
Resolve conflicting intent, stage the result and continue the active operation.
Compare the final diff and run focused tests before proposing any shared reference update.

tasks.name: Predict the graph
steps: Draw A branching into B on main and C on feature. A merge creates M with parents B and C. A rebase creates C-prime with parent B. Mark C and C-prime as different identities even when their logical change is similar.

tasks.name: Resolve an intent conflict
tasks.goal: Preserve behavior rather than one side.
steps: A fictional base sets timeout=10, main changes it to 20 and feature adds a retry deadline of 15. Explain why choosing timeout=20 alone may exceed the total deadline. Propose a coherent timeout/deadline design and state the missing requirement.

tasks.name: Inspect without rewriting
steps: In an existing disposable repository run `git status` and `git log --oneline --graph -5`. These read state only. Identify whether an operation is in progress; do not run continue, abort or reset in a repository containing someone else's work.

tasks.name: Plan conflict recovery
steps: On paper, write merge resolution as edit, test, stage and commit or continue; write rebase resolution as edit, stage and rebase continue, followed by tests. Include the appropriate abort option and prohibit force-pushing shared history without an agreed policy.

key_terms: Merge: integration connecting histories.
Rebase: replay onto a different base.
Fast-forward: reference movement without divergent merge.
Conflict: change combination requiring a decision.
lesson.safety: Use paper graphs and read-only inspection. Never rewrite a shared branch or discard uncommitted work for this exercise.
cleanup: No history mutation is required; retain only the synthetic graph and resolution rationale.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical feature branch is already used by several colleagues. Would you rebase it to resolve a conflict?
interview_points: Check team policy and shared-history dependencies first.
Explain new identities and collaborator reconciliation.
Consider a merge that preserves published commits.
Resolve behavior and test the combined result, not just markers.

git/git-merge-rebase-and-conflict-resolu.core: Merge preserves topology; rebase creates new identities. Respect shared-history policy, inspect active operation state and resolve combined behavior. Textual success is not semantic correctness; verify with focused tests.
objectives: Design conflict resolution that preserves both intents.
prerequisites: Understand commits, branches and the staging index.

storyboard.title: Two valid changes conflict in combination
storyboard.objective: Connect history integration with semantic verification.

scenes.title: Independent edits
scenes.caption: Both branches change related timing behavior.
scenes.narration: Main increases the timeout while the feature adds a total retry deadline. Each change has a separate intended benefit.

scenes.title: Incoherent combination
scenes.caption: A per-attempt timeout can exceed the total deadline.
scenes.narration: Selecting both values without reasoning creates an inconsistent timing contract, even if conflict markers have been removed successfully.

scenes.title: Resolve intent and test
scenes.caption: History integration must preserve a coherent behavior contract.
scenes.narration: The developer chooses compatible timing values from the requirements and tests the combined deadline behavior before publishing the integrated branch.

lesson.title: Git pull requests code review and branch protection
lesson.why: Review is most effective when reviewers can understand the intended change and when approvals apply to the code actually merged. Branch rules turn team expectations into enforceable checks instead of relying on memory.
lesson.what: A pull request proposes integrating one branch into another and gathers review, automated checks and discussion. Repository rules govern who can update protected branches and what evidence is required; they do not replace careful human reasoning.

concepts.name: Reviewable scope
concepts.body: A focused change with clear purpose, risks and test evidence reduces review effort. Distinguish authored code from generated changes and explain compatibility effects. Large unrelated edits make subtle behavioral mistakes harder to notice and delay meaningful feedback.

concepts.name: Required checks
concepts.body: Required checks gate integration on named automation results. A green check is useful only if the workflow tests the relevant code and cannot be trivially bypassed. Distinguish the reviewed head commit from the base branch's changing integration context.

concepts.name: Approvals and ownership
concepts.body: Reviewer assignment and code ownership identify accountable experts. New commits may invalidate earlier approval according to policy. An approval is not permanent certification of every later edit, and resolving a comment should explain the actual change or justified disagreement.

concepts.name: Protected integration
concepts.body: Branch protections or rulesets can require review, restrict pushes and control bypass. Merge queues can test combinations against a changing base. Emergency access should be narrow and auditable, not a routine way around failing checks or unresolved review.

e2e: Prepare a focused branch and describe intent, risks and validation evidence.
Run applicable checks and request reviewers with relevant ownership.
Address feedback and revalidate the exact commit proposed for integration.
Merge only through the configured rules and retain a traceable review and release record.

tasks.name: Write a review brief
steps: For a fictional timeout change, write purpose, expected behavior, failure risks and the smallest useful test. Mark test execution as not performed unless it actually was. Include the before/after values so a reviewer need not infer the requirement.

tasks.name: Evaluate an approval timeline
steps: Offline, approval covers commit A; author then adds B changing authentication. Expected decision: require the applicable checks and renewed review for B under a stale-approval policy. Approval of A is not evidence that B's security behavior was inspected.

tasks.name: Design a rule set
steps: Choose required review, relevant automated checks and restricted direct updates for a hypothetical main branch. Add a named emergency process with recorded rationale and follow-up. Do not enable repository settings or grant bypass permissions during this exercise.

tasks.name: Assess a moving base
steps: Two individually passing changes both alter a shared API. Explain how merging one can invalidate the other's earlier result. Propose testing the combined candidate through an up-to-date check or merge queue rather than assuming isolated green runs compose safely.

key_terms: Pull request: proposed branch integration.
Required check: mandatory automation result.
Code owner: designated reviewer for an area.
Bypass: authorized exception to enforced rules.
lesson.safety: Use fictional review records. Do not open real requests, change branch rules or invent completed test results.
cleanup: Retain the sample review brief and policy; no repository permissions or remote branches were changed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical pull request has approval and green checks, but another change merged into its base afterward. What would you verify?
interview_points: Identify exactly which commit and integration context were checked.
Rerun relevant combined-state validation.
Apply stale-approval and branch rules consistently.
Avoid bypassing a failed check merely to merge faster.

git/git-pull-requests-code-review-and-br.core: Review the exact proposed change with honest test evidence. Required checks, ownership and stale-approval rules guard integration; a moving base can invalidate earlier results. Keep emergency bypass narrow, justified and auditable.
objectives: Explain stale approvals and integration-state checks.
prerequisites: Understand branches, commits and automated tests.

storyboard.title: An approved commit is not every future commit
storyboard.objective: Trace approval validity as a pull request changes.

scenes.title: Commit A is reviewed
scenes.caption: Approval and checks describe a particular candidate.
scenes.narration: The reviewer and checks examine commit A with a known base, providing evidence for that specific integration candidate.

scenes.title: Commit B changes behavior
scenes.caption: Earlier approval does not inspect the new authentication edit.
scenes.narration: The author adds a new authentication change. The prior evidence cannot establish that this later behavior is correct.

scenes.title: Revalidate the candidate
scenes.caption: Apply current review and check requirements before merge.
scenes.narration: The updated candidate receives the required review and integration checks, then passes through the protected merge path without an undocumented bypass.

lesson.title: Git release tags semantic versioning and changelogs
lesson.why: A release label should identify the same source every time. Moving tags or overstating compatibility breaks reproducibility and makes incident recovery harder because users cannot reliably connect a deployed artifact with reviewed changes.
lesson.what: Git tags name objects, commonly release commits. Semantic versioning communicates compatibility of a declared public interface. Changelogs explain user-relevant effects, while build provenance links a tagged source revision to the artifact actually distributed.

concepts.name: Tag types
concepts.body: A lightweight tag is a reference; an annotated tag has its own object with metadata and a message, optionally a signature. Tags do not automatically move when branches advance. Published release tags should remain stable even if a later fix is needed.

concepts.name: Compatibility contract
concepts.body: A major version signals incompatible public-interface changes, a minor version adds compatible functionality and a patch version provides compatible fixes under semantic-versioning conventions. Define the public interface first; an apparently internal change can still break documented behavior or operational assumptions.

concepts.name: Release identity
concepts.body: A source tag alone does not prove which artifact was built or deployed. Record the commit and artifact digest plus build evidence. Rebuilding the same tag with mutable dependencies can produce different bytes, so dependency and toolchain controls matter.

concepts.name: Changelog quality
concepts.body: Write entries for users: behavior changes, migration requirements and important fixes. Separate unreleased work from published versions. Avoid copying every commit subject without context, and never label a release tested or signed unless that evidence actually exists.

e2e: Define the public compatibility contract and classify the release's changes.
Verify the intended commit and create an appropriately documented immutable release tag.
Build under controlled inputs and record the artifact digest with source identity.
Publish accurate release notes and use a new version for subsequent corrections.

tasks.name: Classify versions
steps: Offline, start from stable version 2.4.1. A compatible bug fix becomes 2.4.2; a compatible feature becomes 2.5.0; removing a documented field requires 3.0.0 under this policy. State assumptions rather than guessing from code-line count.

tasks.name: Inspect tags safely
steps: In a disposable repository run read-only `git tag --list` and, for a known local tag, `git cat-file -t TAGNAME` after substituting its actual name. Expect tag for an annotated tag or the referenced object's type for a lightweight tag.

tasks.name: Write a useful release entry
steps: A fictional API replaces field total with total_cents. Write a changelog entry naming the affected clients, unit change and migration action. Do not call it a patch merely because the implementation changed only one line.

tasks.name: Recover from a bad release
steps: A hypothetical version 2.4.2 contains a bug. Propose a new 2.4.3 fix or a deployment rollback to a known artifact, keeping the original tag unchanged. Explain why retagging 2.4.2 would make two consumers report the same name for different code.

key_terms: Annotated tag: metadata-bearing tag object.
Public interface: supported external behavior contract.
Artifact digest: content-derived build identity.
Changelog: user-oriented release change record.
lesson.safety: Use paper releases and read-only Git inspection. Do not create, move or push tags in shared repositories.
cleanup: Retain only fictional version decisions; no releases or artifacts were published.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical released tag points to a buggy commit. Should you move it to the fix while keeping the same version?
interview_points: Preserve published tag identity.
Issue a new version or roll back to a known artifact.
Record source commit and artifact digest.
Explain compatibility and migration impact honestly.

git/git-release-tags-semantic-versioning.core: Keep published tags stable. Version against a defined public contract, not change size. A tag identifies source, while a digest identifies artifact bytes; release notes must describe user impact and only claim verified evidence.
objectives: Explain stable tags versus artifact identity.
prerequisites: Understand commits, tags and public APIs.

storyboard.title: Fix a release without moving its identity
storyboard.objective: Connect stable source tags with reproducible release records.

scenes.title: Release recorded
scenes.caption: A tag, commit and digest describe the delivered artifact.
scenes.narration: The release records source identity and artifact bytes, allowing consumers to identify exactly which build they received.

scenes.title: Retagging creates ambiguity
scenes.caption: One version name could point to different source histories.
scenes.narration: Moving the published tag to a fix would make existing and new consumers use the same label for different code.

scenes.title: Publish a new correction
scenes.caption: Preserve the old record and assign a new release identity.
scenes.narration: The team keeps the original tag, publishes a new fix version and documents the affected behavior and migration guidance.

lesson.title: Git bisect revert and incident recovery
lesson.why: Incident recovery needs both a safe mitigation and reliable evidence about the regression. Git can narrow a faulty change and record an inverse patch, but source history tools do not automatically reverse database or external side effects.
lesson.what: Bisect searches a commit range using a good/bad predicate. Revert creates a new commit undoing a selected change, preserving shared history. Recovery combines these tools with reproducible tests, artifact identity and application-specific rollback constraints.

concepts.name: Binary search evidence
concepts.body: Bisect repeatedly selects a commit between known good and bad points. A deterministic predicate makes the search meaningful. If the symptom is flaky or the environment changed, contradictory results can blame an innocent commit and waste incident time.

concepts.name: Skipped commits
concepts.body: Some revisions cannot be built or tested. Mark them untestable rather than guessing good or bad. Skips near the boundary can leave multiple possible first-bad commits; report that uncertainty instead of claiming an exact cause unsupported by the search.

concepts.name: Revert versus reset
concepts.body: Revert records an inverse change as a new commit, which suits shared history. Reset moves a local reference and can discard work depending on its mode. A merge revert also requires understanding the chosen mainline parent and future merge consequences.

concepts.name: Operational rollback
concepts.body: Undoing code may not undo data migrations, messages or user-visible effects. Prefer the smallest safe mitigation and validate compatibility with current data. Preserve incident evidence and the exact deployed artifact rather than making unreviewed history edits under pressure.

e2e: Preserve the incident state and identify known good and bad source or artifact revisions.
Reproduce the symptom with a deterministic test before beginning a bounded bisect.
Classify each selected revision honestly and stop with an identified or uncertain boundary.
Apply a reviewed revert or other mitigation, then verify behavior against current data and deployment state.

tasks.name: Calculate search depth
steps: For a linear range of 32 candidate commits and an ideal binary search, about log2(32) = five classifications narrow the boundary. Explain that merges, skipped revisions and unreliable tests can require more work or leave ambiguity.

tasks.name: Define a reliable predicate
tasks.goal: Avoid blaming a random flaky result.
steps: A fictional parser should reject negative quantities. Define one fixed input, expected exit or assertion and controlled dependencies. Contrast that test with an internet-dependent latency probe whose result may change even when the commit does not.

tasks.name: Review bisect lifecycle
steps: Write the local sequence: bisect start, mark known bad and good commits, test chosen revisions, mark or skip, then bisect reset. Inspect `git bisect -h` for available commands. Do not start a search in a dirty or shared working tree.

tasks.name: Choose a safe mitigation
steps: A hypothetical release removes a database column and breaks old code. Explain why reverting application code alone may fail. Compare restoring compatibility through a forward migration with deploying a known compatible artifact, and require a specific health check after mitigation.

key_terms: Bisect: commit-range binary search.
Predicate: test deciding good or bad behavior.
Revert: new commit containing an inverse change.
Mainline: parent used to interpret a merge revert.
lesson.safety: Use offline scenarios and command help. Do not reset shared history, discard work or run production rollback commands.
cleanup: No bisect was started here; if using a separate demo later, end its search with bisect reset before removing it.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical bisect points to different commits on repeated runs. How would you respond before reverting anything?
interview_points: Investigate test nondeterminism and changing dependencies.
Verify good and bad endpoints.
Mark untestable revisions honestly.
Separate safe mitigation from an unproven root-cause claim.

git/git-bisect-revert-and-incident-recov.core: Bisect requires stable good/bad evidence; skips may leave ambiguity. Revert preserves shared history but cannot undo every external effect. Verify mitigation against current data and exact deployed artifacts.
objectives: Estimate and design a reliable bisect investigation.
Distinguish source revert from operational rollback.
prerequisites: Understand commit ancestry and repeatable tests.

storyboard.title: A flaky test makes bisect evidence inconsistent
storyboard.objective: Show why regression search needs a stable predicate.

scenes.title: Search a known interval
scenes.caption: Good and bad endpoints bound the candidate range.
scenes.narration: Bisect selects a midpoint and relies on the regression test to classify its behavior consistently under controlled conditions.

scenes.title: Contradictory results
scenes.caption: The same revision alternates between passing and failing.
scenes.narration: An unstable external dependency changes the result. The apparent first-bad commit becomes unreliable because the predicate no longer describes source behavior alone.

scenes.title: Stabilize evidence first
scenes.caption: Control dependencies and repeat the endpoint checks.
scenes.narration: The investigator isolates the predicate, rechecks known endpoints and reports any untestable revisions before using the search result for a proposed revert.

lesson.title: Git secrets signing and repository hygiene
lesson.why: Deleting a secret from the current file does not revoke it or erase earlier copies. Repository hygiene separates credential containment, history cleanup and artifact trust so a cosmetic edit is not mistaken for incident recovery.
lesson.what: Git preserves committed content across history and other clones. Signing provides evidence about who controlled a signing identity for an object; it does not certify that code is safe. Prevention and response need both identity and content controls.

concepts.name: Secret lifecycle
concepts.body: Tokens, private keys and passwords should come from approved secret stores or runtime identity, not tracked files. A leaked credential must be revoked or rotated at its authority. Removing a line from Git cannot invalidate copies already obtained by others.

concepts.name: Ignore limitations
concepts.body: Ignore rules affect untracked file discovery; they do not automatically stop tracking a committed file. Templates should contain obvious placeholders, not plausible working credentials. Review staged changes and generated files because accidental inclusion often occurs outside the main source file.

concepts.name: Signing scope
concepts.body: Signed commits or tags connect an object to a verifiable signing identity under a trust policy. Verification depends on trusted keys or identity rules. A valid signature proves neither code review nor vulnerability freedom, and compromised signing access still requires incident handling.

concepts.name: Coordinated cleanup
concepts.body: History rewriting can remove sensitive material from chosen references but disrupts commit identities and collaborators. Forks, caches and external clones may retain copies. Contain the credential first, then follow the hosting provider's coordinated removal process and preserve necessary incident evidence.

e2e: Prevent sensitive values from entering the working tree and inspect the staged snapshot.
If exposure occurs, revoke or rotate the credential and assess its use immediately.
Coordinate repository-history cleanup and collaborator recovery without pretending all copies disappear.
Verify new access controls and document provenance, signing and remaining exposure uncertainty.

tasks.name: Demonstrate ignore scope
steps: Offline, a tracked config.txt is later added to .gitignore. Expected result: it remains tracked and changes remain visible to Git. Explain why ignoring a filename is not credential rotation or removal from existing commits.

tasks.name: Inspect staged filenames
steps: In a disposable repository run `git diff --cached --name-only`. Review filenames before examining content, and use only synthetic files. Look for generated credentials or local environment files without opening real secrets or copying their values into notes.

tasks.name: Order incident actions
steps: A fictional token was committed and pushed. Rank revocation, access-log review, replacement deployment and coordinated history cleanup. Expected first containment is invalidating the exposed token, not rewriting the last commit while the token remains usable.

tasks.name: Evaluate signed malicious content
steps: A hypothetical signed commit contains an unsafe dependency change. State that its signature can be valid while the change still requires rejection. Add code review, dependency checks and protected signing access rather than treating the signature as a security approval.

key_terms: Revocation: invalidating an issued credential.
Signature: cryptographic evidence tied to an object.
Ignore rule: untracked-path exclusion pattern.
History rewrite: replacement of reachable commit ancestry.
lesson.safety: Use no real tokens, private keys or credential-like samples. Do not scan unrelated repositories or rewrite shared history.
cleanup: Remove only synthetic demo files if created; leave real credentials untouched and route actual exposure through the approved incident process.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical teammate deletes a leaked token and signs the next commit. Is the incident resolved?
interview_points: Revoke or rotate the token at its issuer.
Investigate potential use and retained copies.
Coordinate history cleanup separately.
Explain that signing does not invalidate secrets or certify safe code.

git/git-secrets-signing-and-repository-h.core: Revoke leaked authority before cleaning history. Ignore rules do not untrack existing files. Signatures establish object identity under a trust policy, not code safety; use review, prevention and coordinated cleanup as separate controls.
objectives: Sequence credential containment and repository cleanup.
Explain the limits of ignore rules and signatures.
prerequisites: Understand tracked files, commits and public/private signing keys.

storyboard.title: Deleting a token does not revoke its authority
storyboard.objective: Separate repository cleanup from credential containment.

scenes.title: Token enters history
scenes.caption: Committed values can be copied beyond the current file.
scenes.narration: A token is committed and copied. Its authority comes from the issuer, while Git stores only the token's representation.

scenes.title: Current file is cleaned
scenes.caption: Old copies may remain usable until authority is revoked.
scenes.narration: Deleting the line changes the newest snapshot but does not invalidate earlier copies or remove their ability to authenticate.

scenes.title: Contain at the issuer
scenes.caption: Revoke first, then coordinate cleanup and investigation.
scenes.narration: The incident owner invalidates the token, reviews use and coordinates repository cleanup while acknowledging that external copies may still exist.
